item.title: Psilocybin, LSD, Other Psychedelics Move to FDA Approval
item.description:
Depression

Psilocybin, LSD, Other Psychedelics Move to FDA Approval

Different psychedelics, different speeds, but hope needs evidence.

Posted October 4, 2026

Key points
  • Psilocybin and LSD are advancing through clinical trials. Other psychedelics need more evidence they work.
  • A mystical experience among users may feel transformative, but lasting benefits require proof.
  • Desperate patients who can’t wait deserve carefully considered access and honest explanations of risks.
  • Move quickly with new treatments, but first establish safety and efficacy compared to existing treatments.

Six months before his death at 27, Cindy Crawford’s son Presley Gerber described taking ibogaine for addiction. He hoped to find his way back to himself. His cause of death remains under investigation. His hope deserves respect. People with addiction want their lives back. But an old A.A. saying captures the challenge: “Once you are a pickle, you can never be a cucumber again.” Recovery is possible. Turning back the clock is another matter.

Failed treatments, craving, and suffering can make a new treatment irresistible. Some describe spiritual awakening and turning the clock back with psychedelics. But feeling transformed and sustained recovery are different things.

Listen to patients.

Then test the treatment. Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) help answer what patients deserve to know: Does it work? For whom? For how long? At what risk? Compared with what?

Different Drugs, Different FDA Timetables

Phase 1 studies assess initial safety, tolerability, and dosing. Phase 2 asks whether treatment is promising and warrants larger studies. Phase 3 RCTs examine efficacy, safety, and other outcomes more extensively. With this data, the FDA evaluates and weighs a new treatment's benefits and risks.

Psychedelic drugs are quite different in their effects. While they are often lumped together, they differ in RCT evidence and progress toward FDA approval. Progress in depression and anxiety does not establish efficacy for SUDs. Each drug needs evidence for each condition. Relieving withdrawal or craving is encouraging. Preventing relapse and overdose over months and years is another test.

Esketamine (Spravato) is now FDA-approved for TRD. The FDA added guardrails with supervised administration and monitoring under a REMS safety program. Spravato is a logical comparison. Psilocybin and LSD deserve the same scientific bar; no psychedelic discount nor a psychedelic penalty.

Progress Towards FDA Approval

COMP360 psilocybin met its primary endpoints in two treatment-resistant depression Phase 3 trials. Its sponsor reports a rolling FDA application and initial review is underway. LSD's sponsor also reported positive results from its second Phase 3 GAD trial in September. But company announcements aren’t FDA approval.

Psychedelics: Promise, Progress, and Proof
Source: Mark Gold, MD with permission

A September 29 JAMA Network Open study of 1,964 U.S. adults adds a warning. Across 13 assessed adverse effects, the higher reported adverse-effect rates were among ibogaine or 5-MeO-DMT users. These findings signal concern, but this was not a controlled drug-safety study. Still, limited evidence of benefit alongside greater reported harm deserves attention. Ibogaine also carries a specific cardiac danger: QT prolongation and potentially fatal arrhythmias. Screening and monitoring matter, but cannot make the drug risk-free. RCTs are needed.

The Blindfold Slips

In a double-blind RCT, neither patients nor outcome assessors should know who received the experimental treatment or placebo. The profound psychedelic “trip” makes that difficult.

Randomization still matters. The drug may genuinely help. But failed masking makes it harder to judge how much benefit comes from pharmacology versus expectations, psychological support, or their interaction. Therapists may behave differently if they know who did/did not take the drug, and symptom ratings may also shift.

Orsini and colleagues reviewed 112 randomized trials and found that only 33 even assessed blinding. Psilocybin, LSD, and ayahuasca studies frequently reported blinding failures exceeding 90 percent among participants and raters. This doesn’t prove ineffectiveness, but it weakens confidence in estimates of the drug’s efficacy

University of Michigan’s Dr. Jacob Aday and colleagues propose that RCTs use active placebos that better reproduce a psychedelic’s mental and physical effects, onset, and duration, while remaining safe and avoiding therapeutic effects of their own. Kevin Yang, M.D., and researchers from UCSF, UC San Diego, and Stanford University call for a more aggressive approach to preserving masking in psychedelic clinical trials. In the September 16 JAMA Psychiatry, they proposed carefully selected control cocktails of psychoactive drugs. They also suggest that participants authorize researchers to withhold selected study-design details, making treatment assignment harder to infer. Their argument: An RCT studying an intense psychedelic experience needs a credible, comparably intense control, with similar supervision and monitoring. But these combinations could themselves cause serious adverse effects, including cardiovascular instability and respiratory depression. Whether these risks are justified—and whether the approach works—remains to be established.

Compared to Existing Treatments

Patients also need direct comparisons with established, effective treatments. Head-to-head RCTs—not percentages from unrelated studies—can tell us which treatment works better and for whom.

Head-to-head RCTs with random assignment—not comparisons of percentages from unrelated studies—are needed to determine which treatment works better, for whom, for how long, and at what risk.

Psychedelic mechanism research is advancing. Joshua Siegel and colleagues showed psilocybin temporarily disrupts usual brain network patterns, with some connectivity changes lasting weeks. A new Nature study of 62 adults found brain activity became more aligned with context—music, meditation, or a movie—and tracked feelings of connection and next-day psychological changes. We still need to establish which changes produce lasting recovery.

A Trial Is Different from Self-Treatment

Compass reports that COMP360 psilocybin met its primary endpoints in two Phase 3 trials for treatment-resistant depression. On September 14, Definium announced the second positive Phase 3 LSD trial in GAD. Other psychedelic trials are moving at their own speed.

A positive RCT does not establish the safety or effectiveness of self-treatment. Researchers study a known drug and dose in selected patients, with supervision, monitoring, and follow-up. Taking mushrooms at home or recreational LSD does not reproduce those conditions.

Selection matters. Trials often exclude people with psychosis or bipolar risk; some also exclude active substance use disorders. Results cannot simply be extended to patients the researchers excluded. Safety assessments must also account for those who worsen or drop out.

The safeguards may disappear. The drug’s risks have not taken a vacation.

Some Patients Cannot Wait

Some patients with OUD remain ill despite evidence-based, FDA-approved treatments. Relapse and continued suffering may deepen depression and hopelessness. The President’s executive order calls for faster psychedelic research and development of access pathways.

VA trials can expand access and help establish whether these treatments work. FDA expanded access may permit investigational treatment for serious or life-threatening conditions when satisfactory alternatives are unavailable.

These routes may allow treatment before FDA approval. Access is not proof that it works. Nor does a pathway guarantee that a patient can get the treatment. Patients deserve compassion and access when justified. They also deserve the truth about what we know, what we do not know, and what could go wrong.

Defining Success

Screen carefully. Put safety first. Continue care. Patients in altered states are vulnerable. No sexual contact. No exploitation. No pushing a therapist’s beliefs.

Registries can help identify uncommon harms and track whether improvements last.

For addiction, a memorable trip is not enough. Neither is easier opioid withdrawal. Can patients rebuild their lives? Use less? Function better? Stay in care? Avoid overdose? Survive? How do outcomes compare with established treatments?

We should move quickly enough to help suffering people. But carefully enough to learn what actually works.

Hope deserves a hearing. Patients deserve the evidence to decide.

item.title: Why Trying to Move on From Regrets Can Keep You Stuck
item.description:
Cognition

Why Trying to Move on From Regrets Can Keep You Stuck

Four questions to help you decode regrets and resolve unfinished business.

Posted October 4, 2026

Key points
  • Regrets involve imagining how things might have turned out better if you had made a different decision.
  • Recurring regrets might signal that you have unfinished business to address.
  • Paradoxically, regrets are most intense when opportunities for corrective action remain high.

What is your biggest regret in life? Do you have intrusive thoughts about your regrets? Do you find yourself constantly thinking, “If only…”?

Regret is a cognitive emotion based on self-focused upward counterfactual thinking. In plain English, this means feeling bad about something you did (or didn’t do), while imagining how things might have turned out better if you had made a different decision.

Regrets are unpleasant and, not surprisingly, research has found that they’re correlated with feeling depressed.

Why You Shouldn’t Ignore Your Lingering Regrets

If you find yourself ruminating about regrets, your instinct might be to avoid thinking about them. Perhaps someone gave you this advice: What’s in the past cannot be undone, so you should just ignore your regrets and move on.

But does this suppression strategy work?

For many people, regrets are like that awful song stuck in your head. Ordering yourself to stop thinking about the song puts it right back on repeat.

Having reviewed the research on the psychology of regret, I’ve concluded that regrets are not simply something unpleasant to suppress. Rather, they can be a signal that you have unfinished business to address.

Trying to squash that signal is like turning off a smoke alarm. Even if you succeed, it doesn’t address what set it off.

Your regret may be pointing to something important. Paradoxically, if you want to move past your regret, begin by paying attention to the meanings embedded in it.

Here are four questions you can ask yourself to discern the signals your regrets may be sending you.

Question 1: Is This Regret Actionable?

Your regret might be signaling that there’s some unfinished action you’ve yet to take.

Researchers Neal Roese and Amy Summerville make the surprising claim that regrets are most intense when opportunities for corrective action remain high. They call this the opportunity principle.

In one study, they found that areas of life with greater opportunities for change contained more intense regrets than those with fewer opportunities. So that pesky regretful thought might be telling you there’s something you still need to act on.

Of course, regrets often feel irreversible. Maybe something you did led to the end of a relationship. Maybe an investment resulted in a huge financial loss. Maybe you regret not attending college when you were younger.

The trick is to avoid all-or-nothing thinking. It’s often not the case that you can either change everything or nothing at all. There may be actionable options in between.

For example, you could write an apology letter to someone you hurt, even if it doesn’t restore the relationship. You could educate others about a mistake you made, such as falling for a financial scam. Or, if you regret not attending college, you could pursue classes or workshops now.

You can’t undo what happened, but your regret may be telling you that you can write the next chapter of your life differently.

Question 2: What Is the Moral of the Story?

What if your regret contains a valuable lesson, but you’re treating it like mental spam? You might be missing an important nugget of wisdom.

Ask yourself: What does this experience teach me to do differently next time? What lessons can I pass on to my loved ones?

For example, “I regret staying in that job” could become: “When I’ve been persistently unhappy in a job for six months and my attempts to improve the situation haven’t worked, I’ll actively investigate alternatives.”

Question 3: Are You Engaging in Too Much Positive Thinking?

Your recurring regrets could be an invitation to explore the situation in more detail and arrive at a more balanced conclusion.

Here, I’ll recommend something counterintuitive: You might be engaging in too much positive thinking and not enough negative thinking.

This is especially relevant to regrets about inaction—what you could have done but didn’t.

If only I had taken that job, I would be a lot richer. If only I had pursued that relationship, I would be happier.

The danger is painting an overly rosy picture of imaginary alternatives. We’ll never know with certainty what would have happened. Maybe things would have turned out wonderfully. But, to be balanced, you should also consider what could have gone wrong.

You imagine the job you could have taken, but not the boss you might have hated. The person you should have dated, but not the conflicts you might have had.

The unchosen path can look deceptively smooth when you never had to encounter its potholes.

Question 4: Am I Evaluating My Behavior or Labeling My Character?

Maybe your rumination about regrets is signaling that you need to change the way you’re evaluating your past decisions. There’s a difference between feeling bad about what you did and condemning yourself.

Pay careful attention to what you’re telling yourself. Is it: I made a bad choice or I’m despicable?

The former generates guilt; the latter, shame. Accountability without self-condemnation appears much more psychologically productive than repeatedly prosecuting yourself.

This is where self-compassion can help. Researchers Jia Wei Zhang and Serena Chen found that people assigned to write about their biggest regret from a compassionate perspective reported less negative emotion and greater commitment to personal improvement than those writing about regrets from a different perspective.

If you find it hard to be self-compassionate, try perspective-taking. Imagine the kind words you would say to a friend in your shoes struggling with regret. Or imagine what a kind friend would say to you.

Before putting your past self on trial, consider that you may have made a decision under pressure, had limited information, or simply been younger and less experienced.

The Takeaway

Regrets are distressing. It takes courage to treat them as unfinished business requiring your attention.

But processing your regrets, rather than ignoring them, could help loosen the knots that keep you tethered to your past. You can’t change the objective events of your past, but you can change your relationship with them and develop the freedom to move forward.

item.title: Aging Better: Intergenerational Learning and the Aging Brain
item.description:
Education

Aging Better: Intergenerational Learning and the Aging Brain

Intergenerational learning benefits our legacy, well-being, and longevity.

Posted October 4, 2026

Key points
  • The current understanding of aging can be expanded.
  • Accepting uncertainty allows for mutual growth between older and younger generations.
  • Participating in intergenerational sharing benefits physical and emotional well-being for all ages.

"If you can forgive as well as forget, if you can keep from growing sour, surly, bitter, and cynical... you got it half-licked." –Henry Miller

"Gradually the river grows wider, the banks recede, the water's flow more quietly, and in the end, without any visible break, they become merged in the sea, and painlessly lose their individual being." –Bertrand Russell

We all know the media's demographic description of growing old. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, adults age 65 and older now make up close to 19% of our population, about 65 million older Americans. Solutions to the ups and downs of aging are basically from one template that supposedly fits all. The need to increase geriatric physicians, more over-the-counter brain stimulation, how to ward off scammers, and even certain podcasts questioning the value of our older population. Most well-intentioned advice emphasizes staying fit, being active, and eating healthy foods, including beets. These ideas are stuck in models masked as the end-of-all means to longevity. They don't suit everyone and, in many cases, are profit-driven. Practical strategies are generalized without regard for the many cultural constraints and contexts that can encourage our senior population to take charge of their well-being beyond being told not to fall.

Source: Natasha Rabin, used with permission

What Do Seniors and the Broader Population Think About Aging?

The Pew Research Report (Nov. 11, 2025) cites that when asked what age senior citizens would like to live to if they had the choice, 76% said they want to live to at least 80, while about 29% said they want to make it to 100. On average, Americans in general say they would like to live to be 90-plus years old. When adults of all ages are asked what they think about aging, 73% say they will age well, 67% think about what it will be like to be a senior, and 67% say they are worried and have concerns, especially about mental health, loneliness, and family relations. Regardless, aging is a multifactorial process with an infinite number of determinants, including class, genetics, stress management, exposure to environmental context, etc. But beyond advice based on self-management models, little addresses intergenerational relations and how they affect mental and emotional issues, as well as physical needs. In other words, once you remove the many different factors from the whole system that includes aging in our society, you are left with fragmented perceptions and continued vulnerability. This, however, is where demographics hint at an amazing opportunity to use the existing interdependence within our society. For instance, seniors 65 and older, as indicated in the above-mentioned Pew study, now outnumber teenagers, a shift driven by the baby-boomer generation and declining birth rates. In fact, it is now projected that all children under 18 will be outnumbered by seniors by 2029.

Another factor supporting intergenerational mutual learning: As we get older, the brain prioritizes wisdom over remembering details. Researchers described in a new study suggest the aging brain is adapting, not declining (Washington Post Sept 25, 26). The brains of older people prioritize differently and develop new capacities while older capacities become slightly less available and notably less relevant. The implications for the importance of intergenerational relationships open the door to unheard beneficial consequences and many new valued possibilities. Sharing and mutual learning not only breaks down stereotypes between generations but also strengthens legacy transmission and sets the stage for new decision-making that learns from our intentions and mistakes. This refutes content without context and encourages the infinite opportunity to better understand and share different information and experiences with each other. In fact, social cohesion is an important factor in supporting new possibilities and helping avoid isolation across different developmental stages of our population and increases longevity.

article continues after advertisement
Source: Natasha Rabin, used with permission

There's so much wisdom to share and create viable differences that improve our lifestyle and better advocate for needed changes in our socio-political society. Children and teens are ready to learn and to share different perspectives, historical insights, and new skills such as ecological communication and problem-solving. Everyday intergenerational interactions can share an infinite amount of useful reciprocal information as demonstrated by CNN host Michael Smerconish’s Mingle Project and Nora Bateson, President of the International Batson Institute’s Warm Data Process. Accomplishments and disappointments are part of our evolution. Safe, caring emotional and biological health is a known consequence of relationships across different contexts in our society. For those of us who are aging into our senior years, as well as our youth, there are many advantages that help with lowering depression and motivating physical movement.

How Intergenerational Dialogue Enhances Human Flourishing

Our technological world offers much that intergenerational dialogue can illuminate. That liminal in-between space in relational learning allows what may seem hidden to surface and be heard. Each story changes the other's story, bringing up a certain depth of who we are as human beings. This makes us respond differently to each other and encourages us to tend to each other's needs. Bertrand Russell once said that "to be fulfilling in your life is to make your interests gradually wider and more impersonal until bit by bit the walls of the ego recede and your life becomes increasingly emerged in the universal life quotations." When we are unable to step outside our cultural constraints that impose models of certainty, we isolate ourselves and misunderstand who we and others are. This hides the intuitive part of our mind and body, keeping us from finding and using our inherent interdependency to create improvisational possibilities. We need to stay away from models and shallow solutions, as Ursula K. Le Guin shares in her writings: "Uncertainty drives us forward. The unknown, the unforetold, the unproven, that is what life is based on; ignorance is the ground of thought. Unproof is the ground of action."

Source: Kenneth Silestri, used with permission

A few years ago, I ran a program for teens who had dropped out of school in an urban community. The students were all minorities, while the adjacent senior citizen housing was predominantly white, with many misimpressions of these youth. I arranged for the teens to have lunch with the seniors over several months in the community room and spend time mutually sharing stories with about their childhoods, schooling, kitchens, backyards, friendships, learning, and what it is like to be a teen and a senior. Many contexts overlapped, and there was exceptional warmth and surprises. Overall, both groups learned and respected each other in new and useful ways.

item.title: The Natural Buzz of Daydreaming, With Meaning and Purpose
item.description:
Fantasies

The Natural Buzz of Daydreaming, With Meaning and Purpose

What our daydreams and fantasies reveal about us.

Posted October 4, 2026

Key points
  • We spend up to 50 percent of our waking state consciousness engrossed in daydreaming activities.
  • Our "dreamscape" sparkles with wish-filled imaginings and aspirations of how we'd like things to be.
  • Our fantasies hatch creativities, guidelines and actionable plans for a better, more prosperous future.

Our Own Fantasyland

Unlike Disneyland, our private fantasyland of daydreams requires no commute, no entry fee, or waiting in tedious, endless lines. Faster than the blink of an eye, we enter a wish-filled world, an exclusive, exhilarating dreamscape of our invention. Visitors are welcome by invitation only. At times, however, uninvited “trespassers,” or personally troubling ruminations, defile our otherwise pleasant internal milieux and demand our attention.

Surprisingly, we spend one-third to half of our waking state consciousness daydreaming or fantasizing. What triggers this prolific mental venturing, this rampant escapism? And why do we distract ourselves, meander off task, or listlessly drift through the wilds of our imagination?

Purposeful Daydreaming

Actually, there’s a clear evolutionary advantage to this sizeable investment of our mental resources. Our promenades down fantasy lane have personal meanings and a purpose; they’re not simply random irregularities or neural spasms. Metaphorically, the “hidden universe” of our imagination has specific goals, “a working destination,” unlike the natural universe, which is expanding indefinitely and seemingly without purpose into something yet to be understood.

As you might expect, neuropsychologists have identified the personal significance, value, and purpose of our dreamy meanderings and sundry, fancified reconstructions of reality customized to achieve our needs and desires.

Well-Orchestrated Daydreaming

A symphony orchestra has four main sections of musical instruments: strings, woodwind, brass, and percussion, all working harmoniously in concert to create its musical spectacles. Likewise, daydreams are a “symphony” of harmonious, well-coordinated neural activity rising from several parts of our brain working in concert. The medial forebrain bundle, the hippocampus, the posterior cingulate cortex, the parietal cortex, and the visual cortex are relevant parts of our brain that coordinate 20-watt energies to light up our fantasy-filled, yet purposeful, mental “adventure park.”

Unleashed from the activities and demands of the real world—or because of them—we find refuge in a relaxed, reflective, or inwardly focused mode of thought, ripe for fantasizing. Now, the pertinent sections of our brain orchestrate respective roles as executive director and sensory, cognitive mediators of free-flowing images, what’s called our “default-neural-network,” a system that produces uncoaxed, spontaneous imaginings.

What follows is a richly textured “symphony” of self-reflections, recountings and revisions of the ups and downs of our personal history, fictitious, often glamorized narratives that are self-gratifying or self-aggrandizing, idealized problem-solving, and visions of past, present, and future events, all performed in the service of the self, for an audience of one.

article continues after advertisement

Morita Philosophy

Japanese psychiatrist Shoma Morita philosophized that humankind possesses a universal, innate need for acceptance and love. However, in our disheartening moments, when we sink into self-doubt and question how acceptable or lovable we are, often the quickest, most palliative remedy is to take flight into fantasy. Here, we may achieve in our “self-medicating,” subjective world what we perceive we lack in the objective world: acceptance, love, and admiration. And more, we can “guarantee” these, risk-free, via our praise-attracting, and self-aggrandizing imagined accomplishments that hail the adulation of others, especially highly valued others, those who count the most.

Winning the Lotteries

A variety of perceived personal defects and insufficiencies, particularly love, relationships, money, status, and personal power, are potent incubators of compensatory fantasizing. To fill these privations, we bask in our dream world adorned with fulfilled desires and ambitions. Common fantasies, especially among younger fantasizers, are winning the monetary and sexual-romantic lotteries.

Optimally, however, our daydreams ought to eventually hatch solutions to problems or actionable plans that can guide our behavior and be applied to a yet unlived, longed-for, idyllic future, one that is more agreeable, gratifying and successful, one more personally fulfilling than our present circumstances.

Emotional Analgesics

Our daydreaming or fantasy reconstructions of reality can be a quick-acting analgesic, an immediate relief from the frustrating shortfalls, prickly disappointments, distresses and pains of daily life. They offer an instant defense, a reliable, rerouting escape from reality’s sometimes hurtful, insufferable adversities. Moreover, like our homes, our daydreams are furnished with emotional creature comforts; they confer security, respite and renewal, comforts that aren’t always easily reached while navigating the sometimes discomforting vagaries of the outer world.

article continues after advertisement

Fantasy Overdosing

However, as with conventional analgesics, dosage levels count. We should be cautious of “overdosing,” so our excursions into fantasyland are temporary, self-informing and productive visits—not prolonged and overstayed. Fantasyland must not become a permanent place of residence, where we chronically insulate ourselves, or worse, isolate ourselves from the outside world. Regrettably, daydreaming becomes psychopathological when overused as a substitute “treatment” for a range of mental disorders, including anxiety and depression.

Our fantasy life ought to be well-tempered, self-titrated or administered in amounts that promote personal welfare and eventual actions that pilot growth and development.

Youth, Aging and Daydreams

Advancing age seems to diminish the frequency of our daydreaming. Young people, however, are big consumers of daydreaming’s “illustrious products,” the imagined treasures, thrills, conquests, and “truckloads” of daring exploits and heroics. For adolescents, their life story is unwritten; it still lies ahead, and fantasizing can fill the “blank slate” outstretched before them with a wish list for a bright, enviable future. But as our life expectancy wanes, so does the need to fancifully fill in what remains of our future. It’s likely older individuals who have realized many of their lifetime aspirations don’t have the same need for fantasy—with perhaps the exception of wanting to be young again or re-doing parts of their past lives.

Pop Quiz

What are your most frequent fantasies or daydreams? What do they reveal about you? Do you feel you’re lacking something or aspiring to something more? If so, do you think your daydreams may provide the impetus you need to achieve them?

item.title: Cracking the Code of Cold People
item.description:
Relationships

Cracking the Code of Cold People

Handling perceived coldness with poise builds inner strength and relationships.

Posted October 4, 2026

Key points
  • Whether intentional or not, cold behavior conveys the message that you are not seen, heard, or appreciated.
  • Perceived coldness can be hard to sit with when you are feeling anxious; this may lead to false assumptions.
  • It's important to remember there are many reasons why people can unintentionally come off as cold.
  • You can acknowledge unmet expectations for warmth, share your own cold moments, and use your energy wisely.
Source: Marina Shatskih/Unsplash

I sent my doctor an article that explained my symptoms. His response: “Response reviewed. No need to respond.”

I showed a friend my latest painting. She said, “I hope you’re happy with it,” without saying whether she liked it.

When I texted other members of a parent group about going to a carnival together, nobody commented on my suggestion.

These are examples of gripes I’ve heard from friends and clients. I, too, have experienced similar responses that can be described as “cold,” and sometimes no responses at all.

Cold behavior isn’t necessarily malicious, but, whether intentional or not, it conveys the message that you are not seen, heard, or appreciated. Cold behavior can trigger unsettling feelings, especially in individuals with trouble tolerating uncertainty about what others think of them.

Research has shown, for example, that people with social anxiety are more likely to misinterpret neutral faces as angry, which suggests that, in anxious people, cold behavior can trigger the brain’s threat detection system (threat sensitivity) to issue false alarms.

Negative assumptions, such as believing you did something to make the person act coldly towards you, or that the person is a jerk, can lead to self-sabotaging behavior that results in feeling more isolated. For example, one might assume another person’s apparent coldness is calculated or intentionally passive-aggressive and respond with passive-aggressive behavior such as ignoring the person you perceived as ignoring you.

Alternatively, one might respond with excessive people-pleasing to ensure they are in the “cold” person’s good graces. Obsequious behavior, though, can become exhausting and feel inauthentic to everyone, to those performing it as well as to those at the receiving en. Sometimes it can become a vicious cycle of misinterpreted signals.

article continues after advertisement

If the chill of someone’s interpersonal behavior is getting under your skin, consider that coldness is temporary and unintentional. People can come across as cold because they are tired, stressed, distracted, or aren’t strong at facial recognition. And there are numerous other reasons!

People with the need for excessive self-control might come off as cold by lacking facial expressiveness and being reticent to share opinions or other personal information.

Medical conditions can also lead to people being misinterpreted as cold. For example, Parkinson’s Disease and other neurological conditions can affect the ability to convey emotion through facial expressions, gestures, and tone of voice, as well as to recognize emotion in others’ faces. People don’t always disclose their medical conditions, which is why we can give people the benefit of the doubt.

Of course, persistent cold behavior can be part of a narcissistic personality, or another personality disorder or style, meaning that your feeling of unease may indicate a toxic situation or calculated response. Responding effectively to a bully, for example, demands maintaining composure to understand and effectively manage distress triggered by this kind of cold behavior.

Consider the following strategies for facing cold behavior with poise:

  1. Distinguish behavior from the person. Consider that the interaction might be a cold moment, as opposed to defining the individual’s entire personality. The latter interpretation may lead to unwarranted distrust of others.
  2. Acknowledge disappointment and update expectations. Assumptions about cold behavior include believing that the person thinks they are better than you or that they dislike you. These assumptions can trigger resentment, anxiety, and sadness.
article continues after advertisement

It can help to reframe this emotional pain as disappointment caused by your expectation for warm behavior being left unmet. Another assumption is believing that you should earn warmth from others through your accomplishments, such as believing that once you climbed the career ladder, the CEO would start responding to your emails quickly and enthusiastically.

Once you acknowledge disappointment, you can revise expectations, which will temper the emotional heaviness of cold interactions.

  1. Model yourself when you show cold behavior. When I’m put off by cold behavior, I find it helpful to take note of instances when I might have come off as cold, such as when I felt rushed or stressed.

In such instances, it’s helpful to acknowledge cold behavior, such as saying, “Sorry I didn’t stick around to chat. I was running late for an appointment.” “I didn’t mean to ignore what you said. I was thinking about some test results I just received.”

Simple explanations might encourage others to share the reasons behind their own cold moments.

4. Use your energy wisely. Ask yourself, “How much does this matter?” “Is this person worth my time and energy?”

If the answer is “yes,” you might respond with more warmth, such as asking if they are okay, or telling them with curiosity that you’ve noticed a change in their behavior.

If the answer is “It doesn’t matter that much,” accept that you can’t control how they think or behave. You don’t necessarily have to break off the friendship, although in toxic relationships, this may be the healthiest response. Know when to let go, such as when a relationship is exhausting or harmful. While challenging, managing this balance might lead to unexpected friendships, and at the very least to greater self-knowledge and inner strength.

Ultimately, nurturing relationships requires hanging in there and committing to improving the connection even when apparent coldness makes us feel our most vulnerable.
